OpenCode Shell Permissions

In OpenCode V2, set shell to ask for all commands, then put specific allow or deny exceptions below it. If a command skips the prompt, check the last matching rule, saved approvals and whether the runner used --auto. Run OpenCode Serve locally.

  1. Set Shell permission rules
  2. Diagnose a missing prompt
  3. Check a combined command
  4. Verify in a scratch repository
  5. See the test results

Set OpenCode V2 Shell permission rules

Run opencode --version in the project. This example uses V2's permissions array and shell action. V1 uses permission and bash. Back up your current configuration and merge these entries into your existing opencode.jsonc.

{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "permissions": [
    { "action": "shell", "resource": "*", "effect": "ask" },
    { "action": "shell", "resource": "git status *", "effect": "allow" },
    { "action": "shell", "resource": "git push *", "effect": "deny" }
  ]
}

Put the broad rule before its exceptions. V2 takes the last matching rule at this stage. The trailing * in git status * matches both git status and git status --short. Check agent rules if the effective policy differs. Review commands in an interactive session when you want to decide one request at a time.

This policy controls the OpenCode Shell tool. Shell commands that receive permission still run with the host user's access to files, processes and the network. Keep secrets out of a trial repository and use OS or container isolation when testing untrusted code.

What happened to the Shell command?

Check approvalsSplit commandsTest safely

Why a command ran without asking

  1. Check the exact command shown in the tool result and compare it with the installed agent's rules. An earlier ask can be followed by a matching allow.
  2. Check whether you selected Allow always for this command or prefix. V2 saves matching approvals for the project, so a new conversation can still use them. Choose Allow once when approval should cover one request.
  3. In an unattended run, check whether the caller passed --auto. Compare a single harmless command in a clean project and an interactive session without auto approval before changing production rules.

Why a combined command was blocked

A compound command can have more than one permission check. git status --short && git log -1 includes a separate git log request, so the git status exception alone gives no permission for the full command. Run each harmless command separately to see which asks or fails.

Check the working directory first if the tool uses an outside path. V2 may check external_directory before the Shell rule. Add a separate ask rule for outside-project access when you want that prompt. Rule matching and directory inference are only one part of deciding whether a command can run safely.

Verify what ran in a scratch repository

  1. Create a disposable Git repository with an initial commit and an untracked permission-check.txt file. Apply the sample rules. Request only git status --short and check that the tool output includes ?? permission-check.txt.
  2. In a separate turn, request only git log -1. In the interactive client, check for a permission prompt and choose Reject for this test. For unattended automation, inspect tool events rather than relying on the exit code.
  3. To exercise a deny without contacting a remote, add a final test rule for printf * with effect deny in the scratch config. Request git status --short && printf BLOCKED_MARKER. Check the Shell tool result and verify that no command output contained the marker. A tool error can quote the requested command itself.

For file writes and V1 setup, see the OpenCode project review. To find the active configuration, see OpenCode config locations.

What OpenCode 2.4.1 did in the Shell checks

We ran six unattended checks on macOS arm64 with a synthetic model server on localhost. Each case used a fresh repository and profile.

  • git status and git status --short both completed and listed the scratch file under the same rule.
  • git log -1 returned a permission error because the unattended process could not ask. Putting shell * → ask after the status exception produced the same error for git status --short.
  • The combined request containing the denied printf returned Permission denied: shell with no command output. The explicit deny also held with --auto in a separate test.

OpenCode exited with status 0 in all six cases. In the JSON output, check the tool_use record with part.tool set to shell. part.state.status distinguished completed from error. Download the recorded rules and results.

See the official permissions reference for the Shell scanner and saved approvals, and the policies reference for administrator-enforced denials.
